title: Piano Concerto No. 1 in E-flat major
hook: Under twenty minutes of fireworks, four movements without a break, and a triangle that scandalised a critic.

painting.title: Liszt at the Piano
painting.collection: Alte Nationalgalerie, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin
painting.pairingNote: Liszt at 29, the most famous pianist in Europe, playing to a circle of writers and musicians in Paris; the years when he was working on this concerto.

facts: Liszt worked on the concerto for more than twenty years. Its main themes are in a sketchbook from around 1830, when he was about nineteen; he finished a version in 1849, kept revising it and published it in 1856.
It was first played in Weimar on 17 February 1855, with Liszt at the piano and Hector Berlioz conducting. Liszt dedicated it to the pianist and composer Henry Litolff.

The four movements are short and follow each other without a break. Themes from one movement return, changed, in the others, and Béla Bartók called the concerto “the first perfect realisation of cyclic sonata form”.

The triangle has a solo in the third movement, and the critic Eduard Hanslick mocked the work as a “Triangle Concerto”. There is also a story, told as a joke, that Liszt and Hans von Bülow fitted the words “None of you understand this, ha-ha!” to the opening notes.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a defiant motto and thundering octaves (I), a dreamy nocturne (II), a sparkling scherzo with triangle (III), a march that brings all the themes back (IV).

movements.heading: Allegro maestoso
movements.summary: The strings hurl out a short, defiant motto and the piano answers at once with thundering octaves. A tender duet with the clarinet brings calm, then the drama returns. The movement does not end loudly: it fades away to the softest sound.

mainIdeas.name: The motto
mainIdeas.description: a short, bold figure in the strings, answered by blazing wind and brass chords.

mainIdeas.name: The falling octaves
mainIdeas.description: fast octaves on the piano, sliding down by semitones.

mainIdeas.name: The duet
mainIdeas.description: a quiet, tender melody shared by the piano and a solo clarinet.

stops.hear: The strings play a short, bold figure, answered by loud chords from the woodwinds and brass
stops.happening: The motto theme of the concerto

stops.hear: The piano crashes in with thundering octaves that sweep across the keyboard
stops.happening: The piano’s first entry, almost a [[cadenza|cadenza]]

stops.hear: The motto again, tossed between piano and orchestra
Quiet and tender: the piano and a solo clarinet play a peaceful duet
The motto returns, louder and more urgent
The piano plays fast, falling octaves that slide down note by note
stops.happening: A falling [[chromatic-scale|chromatic scale]] in octaves; it will return in the third and fourth movements

stops.hear: Earlier music comes back in a new key
stops.happening: A return of the opening material, now in G major

stops.label: Last 45 seconds
stops.hear: The strings play the motto softly while the piano ripples like a harp; a rising scale fades to almost nothing

notice: Listen to how the movement ends: after all the thunder, it vanishes. Liszt keeps the loud ending for the very end of the concerto.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Richter recorded both Liszt concertos with Kondrashin and the London Symphony Orchestra over three days in July 1961, soon after his London debut. On the Spotify album this concerto is tracks 1–4.

movements.heading: Quasi adagio
movements.summary: A slow, dreamy song. The low strings introduce it, and the piano takes it up like a [[nocturne|nocturne]]. After a climax and a silence, the mood breaks: the piano answers the orchestra in free, speech-like phrases, then trills while the woodwinds sing a new tune.

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a slow, singing melody, first in the [[muted|muted]] cellos and basses.

mainIdeas.name: The new tune
mainIdeas.description: a gentle melody passed from one woodwind to another over the piano’s trills.

stops.hear: Muted cellos and basses play a slow, singing line; the other strings join
stops.happening: The theme of the slow movement

stops.hear: The piano enters softly with a dreamy melody over flowing left-hand arpeggios
The music swells to a strong climax, then falls away in a long scale
stops.happening: The climax, followed by a silence

stops.hear: The orchestra begins again, restless; the piano answers in free, speech-like phrases
Flute, oboe and clarinet take turns with a new tune while the piano holds long [[trill|trill]]s
stops.happening: Woodwind solos over the piano’s trills

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Piano and clarinet in a quiet duet; the music runs straight on
stops.happening: The link to the third movement

notice: Follow the piano’s long trills near the end. The woodwinds sing above them, so the piano becomes a shimmering background instead of the soloist.

movements.heading: Allegretto vivace – Allegro animato
movements.summary: A sparkling [[scherzo|scherzo]] that starts with a solo for triangle. The piano plays a light, mischievous tune with the woodwinds, until the music darkens and old themes return. The movement ends with a fierce piano passage that stops on a tense, unresolved chord.

mainIdeas.name: The scherzo tune
mainIdeas.description: a quick, playful melody on the piano, marked *capriccioso scherzando* (whimsical and joking).

mainIdeas.name: The return
mainIdeas.description: the motto and the falling octaves from the first movement.

stops.hear: A few strokes on the triangle, then light strings
stops.happening: The scherzo begins. This is the solo that made Hanslick mock the “Triangle Concerto”

stops.hear: The piano plays a quick, playful tune
Woodwinds and piano trade light, teasing phrases
Darker: the piano trembles low down while a theme from earlier is heard quietly above
The falling octaves return, now quietly
A rising sweep in the orchestra, and the motto returns with full force
stops.happening: *Allegro animato*: the opening of the concerto comes back

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A blistering piano passage that stops on a tense, unresolved chord
stops.happening: It leads straight into the finale

notice: The movement ends on a chord that does not resolve. The answer comes only when the finale begins.

movements.heading: Allegro marziale animato
movements.summary: The finale turns the slow movement’s dreamy song into a brisk march. Then themes from the whole concerto return one after another, faster and brighter, and the piano drives towards a dazzling end in E-flat major.

mainIdeas.name: The march
mainIdeas.description: the slow movement’s song, now quick and military, in the woodwinds.
The falling octaves, now at breakneck speed.

stops.hear: A falling scale, then the slow movement’s tender song as a brisk march in the winds
stops.happening: [[thematic-transformation|Thematic transformation]]: the same tune in a new character

stops.hear: The piano alone, with dazzling octaves
Light, dainty exchanges between the piano and solo woodwinds
stops.happening: Earlier themes return in new forms

stops.hear: Themes from all the movements follow one another
A new, sliding theme; the piano plays two rhythms at once with the strings
Faster: the falling octaves at breakneck speed

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: Octaves moving apart in both hands, a huge E-flat major; the orchestra alone has the last two notes

notice: Listen to the last two notes. The piano has stopped, and the orchestra closes the concerto on its own.

threads.title: One set of themes
threads.body: The motto, the falling octaves and the slow song return across the movements, each time in a new form. This is the [[cyclic-form|cyclic form]] Bartók admired.

threads.title: Transformation
threads.body: The tender song of the slow movement becomes a march in the finale. Liszt changes a theme’s character while keeping its notes.

threads.title: The virtuoso
threads.body: Liszt wrote the concerto for his own hands. Its octaves and leaps show off the pianist who was the most famous performer of his age.
